title: Doubling Down on the Importance of Teaching Students to Recognize Terms
author: Julie Pottinger
summary: Julie Pottinger, a 7th grade math teacher, argues that teaching students to see the "terms" of an expression is the key to understanding mathematical structure. She ties the idea to the root "term," meaning boundary, and shows that numerical expressions share the same structure as algebraic ones. On her view, teaching the order of operations through PEMDAS-style rules obscures that structure, because the rules are not arbitrary but flow from how terms are built. She explains how students misread the minus sign as a standalone operator, and how she corrects this by teaching that a number is either positive or negative and that the minus sign means "the opposite." Examples and non-examples, such as asking how many terms two similar-looking expressions have, helped students see boundaries. She tests whether her approach caused algebra struggles by observing an intervention class and finds that the struggling students were mostly not hers and that their errors were the same dropped-minus-sign misunderstandings. She closes by inviting scrutiny of her reasoning while remaining committed to teaching terms first.
points: Seeing an expression as a set of signed terms explains why we simplify the way we do and makes the order of operations a consequence of structure instead of a list of rules.
Students who treat the minus sign as a stand-alone "distance" operator, rather than as belonging to the term that follows, make persistent errors with negative values.
Teaching with non-examples, such as expressions that look like they have three terms but have two, quickly sharpens students' sense of where a term's boundary lies.
Pottinger checked whether her method had caused later algebra difficulties and found the struggling students were largely ones she had not taught, which supports the approach without proving it.
Her stance of publishing reasoning so that cracks can be found early models a healthy professional habit of testing teaching ideas openly.
quotes: We need to stop teaching PEMDAS, not just because it creates more problems than it solves, but because our focus on teaching the order of operations has superseded the focus on structure that we should be teaching instead.

Students see the subtraction symbol as a standalone operator telling them to find the “distance” between the numbers that appear on either side, rather than a symbol that applies to and is connected to the term that follows.
The equal sign means “is the same as.” In other words, subtracting b is the same as adding a “negative b.” The equal sign does not mean “should become.
Predictably, given that I had introduced terms only in the affirmative (this is a term) and never with a non-example
When I posed a similar question the following day, I was pleasantly surprised to see that students retained this understanding
As it turned out, the majority of students who were struggling were not students I had previously taught.
The students were ignoring or dropping or misunderstanding minus signs left and right, particularly when the value substituted for x or y was negative.
But I am convinced that once you see the terms you can’t unsee them, and they are the key to unlocking and understanding mathematical structure.
